question_text: Solve dy/dx + y tan x = sin x.

insider_note: secx sinx simplifies to tanx before integrating — cancel the common cos x underneath sec x and inside sin x/cos x rather than integrating sec x sin x as a product.

steps.label: Identify P and find ∫P dx
steps.margin_note: One mark. The equation is already in the standard linear form dy/dx + Py = Q.
steps.memory_tip: The coefficient of the plain y term, tan x, is P; sin x on its own is Q.
lines: Given D.E is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
This is a linear D.E in y.
Here P = tan x ⇒ ∫P dx = ∫tan x dx = log sec x
steps.why: The equation is already written as dy/dx + yP = Q, so identifying P as the coefficient of y and integrating it is the direct first step every linear-equation solution follows.
common_mistakes: Confusing P with Q and taking P = sin x instead of tan x.
Integrating tan x incorrectly and missing the log sec x form.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx) always.
steps.memory_tip: e^(log sec x) = sec x — the exponential undoes the log immediately.
lines: ∴ I.F. = e^(∫P dx) = e^(log sec x) = sec x
steps.why: The integrating factor formula e^(∫P dx) applies to every linear equation, and here it simplifies at once because e and log are inverse operations.
common_mistakes: Writing I.F. = sec x + tan x by confusing this with the integrating factor for P = sec x seen elsewhere in the chapter.
Forgetting the e^(...) step and writing I.F. = log sec x directly.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: Two marks. sec x · sin x simplifies to tan x, which integrates directly to log sec x.
steps.memory_tip: sec x sin x = sin x/cos x = tan x — cancel before integrating, not after.
lines: Hence the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
⇒ y sec x = ∫sec x·sin x dx = ∫tan x dx

lines.text: y sec x = log sec x + c

steps.why: Writing sec x · sin x as tan x turns the right-hand integral into the same standard tan x integral used in step 1, giving the final relation between y, x and the constant directly.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate sec x · sin x as a product rule instead of simplifying it to tan x first.
Stopping at y sec x = ∫tan x dx without carrying out the integral to log sec x.
